explain.say: Imagine writing a birthday card to your cousin in another city. You drop it in a postbox, and a day or two later it lands on their doormat. How? Look at the first stage. Your letter needs an address, a postcode and a stamp, which shows you've paid for the journey.

faq.q: Why does a letter need a stamp?
faq.a: The stamp shows the cost of the journey has been paid. Before stamps, the person who got the letter often paid. The first sticky stamp was Britain's Penny Black in 1840.
asks: What was the first postage stamp?

faq.q: How do machines read addresses on letters?
faq.a: Cameras photograph each envelope, and software reads the address and postcode, even handwriting. The machine prints a code so later machines can sort it quickly.

faq.q: How long does a letter take to arrive?
faq.a: Inside many countries, one to three days. Letters to other countries can take a week or more.

faq.q: Why do letters need a postcode?
faq.a: A postcode, or PIN code in India, tells sorting machines which area and round a letter belongs to, so it can be sorted in seconds.

faq.q: What happens to a letter with a wrong address?
faq.a: Sorting staff try to work it out. If they can't, it may go back to the sender's address, or to a special office for mail that can't be delivered.
asks: What if I write the wrong address?

facts: The Penny Black, issued in Britain in 1840, was the world's first adhesive postage stamp.
Modern mail sorting machines read addresses with cameras and can sort tens of thousands of letters an hour.
